title: Krishna Sinks the Chariot
story:
The duel Karna and Arjuna had been waiting for all their lives came at last, and for a long time no one could say who was winning. Everything hung on this duel, and both armies knew it. Arjuna's weapon had been swelling with energy and careering through the sky like lightning, consuming the Kauravas, and the broken divisions of their army had drawn back to a distance to watch it — until Karna crushed it with shafts winged with gold, using the great foe-killing weapon he had obtained from Rama, and turned it back. Then he bent his own loud-sounding bow, whose string could not be broken, and sent showers of shafts that pierced Arjuna again and again.

So the two of them closed with each other, and the sky went dark. They struck like two fierce elephants locking tusks. The points of the compass vanished behind their weapons, and the sun itself disappeared beneath the downpour of arrows, until the whole welkin was one vast web of shafts with no space between. The men watching from both armies could see nothing but arrows, and no one on either side could tell where the next one would come from. Two warriors, both accomplished in the use of weapons, wove every kind of beautiful manoeuvre, each of them watching for the other's single lapse — the one opening that would end it.

Now the son of the charioteer would press his rival back, now the diademed Arjuna would drive him in turn. The beings gathered in the sky shouted first "Excellent, O Karna!" and then "Excellent, O Arjuna!" while the earth was pressed deep beneath the weight of the cars and the trampling of steeds and elephants. It was a passage of arms so dreadful that the other warriors on the field could only stand and wonder.

And in that darkness of arrows, something else was waiting for its opening too. The snake Aswasena had long been hostile to Arjuna, and he had been sheltering in the arrow-net above the field, biding his time. Now he let himself be fitted to a shaft, and Karna, bending his loud-sounding bow, loosed him at Arjuna's head.

The shaft blazed as it flew through the welkin, alive and burning, aimed to end the duel at a stroke.

Krishna saw it coming — the way a man who has driven a thousand chariots sees the one arrow among ten thousand that matters.

With great speed and the greatest ease, he pressed down the chariot with his feet. The excellent car sank about a cubit into the earth, and the white steeds, white as the rays of the moon, bent their knees and laid themselves down on the ground.

The burning arrow passed low over Arjuna's head, close enough to graze it — and swept away only his diadem.

The crown fell to the earth, and the man who had worn it was still standing. The diadem was the mark by which the whole field knew Arjuna, and Karna's deadliest shaft had torn it from his head and left the head itself untouched. It had met a charioteer who would sink the very ground beneath his friend to keep that head upon his shoulders. In the middle of the greatest battle the world had ever seen, the moment that saved Arjuna came down to a man setting his feet a cubit deeper into the earth. The chariot rose again, the moon-white horses came back to their feet, and the duel went on — but the opening had passed, and it had passed because of the man holding the reins. Krishna had raised no weapon that day. He had not needed one.
reflection: The episode makes Krishna's loyalty literal: he is not fighting, not speaking, only driving, and yet the whole outcome turns on his feet pressing a chariot into the earth. The divine protection here is not a weapon or a miracle of light but a quick, precise act of a charioteer who will not let his friend be taken.
content_note: Battle violence; an arrow narrowly misses Arjuna.
next_story_tease: But the duel between Karna and Arjuna was not yet decided.
hero_scene: Krishna, reins in hand, presses the chariot down into the earth with his feet as the white horses kneel, while Karna's blazing snake-arrow sweeps just over Arjuna's bowed head and knocks the diadem from his hair.
